Workmanship
wŭrk'man-shĭp
n. (the skill of a workman; the thing made, considered as the product of that skill)
English workman and -ship, the suffix of condition or quality. The Greek poiema in Ephesians 2:10 is the noun behind English poem: a thing made.

Biblical Definition

Twice the word is used of the Spirit's gift to Bezaleel: “I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” (Exo 31:3), repeated when Moses announces it to the congregation (Exo 35:31), with the particulars given in Exodus 31:5 — in cutting of stones, to set them, and in carving of timber. The tabernacle was not thrown together; it was made by a Spirit-filled artist to a pattern shewed in the mount. The word also has a dark use. Ahaz saw an altar at Damascus and sent Urijah the priest “the fashion of the altar, and the pattern of it, according to all the workmanship thereof” (2Ki 16:10), and the brasen altar of the LORD was moved aside to make room for a copy of a pagan design. Excellent workmanship in the service of a borrowed religion is still apostasy. And Paul takes the idea to its height: “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works” (Eph 2:10) — the Greek is poiema, His piece of work, His making. The believer is not the craftsman of his own salvation; he is the object on the bench.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines workmanship as the skill of a workman; the art or skill with which a thing is made; also the work performed; that which is effected by manual labor or skill.

expand to see more

WORKMANSHIP, n. Manufacture; something produced by manual labor.

2. The skill of a workman; the execution or manner of making any thing.

3. That which is effected, made or produced; as, we are his workmanship. Eph. ii.

Key Scripture

Exo 31:3 — "And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,"

2Ki 16:10 — "And king Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, and saw an altar that was at Damascus: and king Ahaz sent to Urijah the priest the fashion of the altar, and the pattern of it, according to all the workmanship thereof."

Eph 2:10 — "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them."

Modern Corruption

Ephesians 2:10 is regularly quoted as a compliment to the reader — you are God's masterpiece — when Paul wrote it to explain why salvation cannot be of works.

expand to see more

Ephesians 2:10 has become a slogan of self-esteem, printed on wall art and read as a statement about the reader's inherent value: you are God's masterpiece. Paul's sentence is doing something quite different, and the connective word at its head shows it. Verses 8 and 9 have just said that by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. Verse 10 gives the reason: for we are his workmanship. The argument is that a made thing cannot take credit for its own making. The chapter began with dead in trespasses and sins, and the whole passage is about a creation out of nothing — created in Christ Jesus. Then the good works appear, not as the ground of salvation but as its purpose and God's prior appointment: which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. Read as intended, the verse humbles before it comforts, and comforts far more deeply than the slogan does. A masterpiece that made itself would be an anxious thing, always needing to prove the claim. A workmanship is safe in the hands of the Workman, and Philippians 1:6 gives the guarantee: he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mela'kah (H4399), work, occupation, workmanship; Greek poiema (G4161), a thing made, that which is fashioned; Greek ktizo (G2936), to create, of the new creation in Christ.

expand to see more

Hebrew mela'kah (H4399) — work, business, workmanship; the word for the tabernacle labour and for the work God rested from on the seventh day; Exodus 31:3, Genesis 2:2.

Greek poiema (G4161) — a thing made, a work; used twice, of the creation that leaves men without excuse and of the believer; Romans 1:20, Ephesians 2:10.

Greek ktizo (G2936) — to create; the new man created in righteousness and true holiness; Ephesians 2:10, 4:24, 2 Corinthians 5:17.

Usage

"“In all manner of workmanship” — the Spirit's gift to the tabernacle craftsman."

"“According to all the workmanship thereof” — Ahaz copying a Damascus altar with excellent skill."

"“We are his workmanship” — the reason salvation cannot be of works."
